one_liner: Stateless key-based R RNG package with C core; xoshiro256++ fills ~2.3x dqrng, ~8x runif(), thread-count-independent output.
what_it_does: An R package (C core, MIT) for reproducible random numbers without global state: you create an immutable key with rng_key(seed) and call rng_uniform(key, n), rng_normal(key, n), rng_integer() or rng_bits(); draw i is a pure function of (key, i), so results do not depend on call order, n, thread count or platform, and .Random.seed is never touched. Substreams come from key vectors or rng_fold(key, "name"), rng_lazy_uniform()/rng_lazy_normal() return ALTREP vectors computed on read, and inst/include/zurand.h gives LinkingTo packages thread-safe fills into their own buffers plus chunked stream_normal()/stream_uniform() callbacks. It is a different interface from runif()/rnorm(), not a drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: The default engine runs a xoshiro256++ recurrence (about five operations per word) on 512-word sub-chunks, each seeded by one Philox4x64-10 call from (key, sub-chunk index); independent sub-chunks are what let it run four lanes of AVX2 (runtime dispatch through a target("avx2") attribute) or eight NEON lanes plus two scalar streams on arm64, and split across OpenMP threads with bit-identical output. Uniforms are converted in registers by mantissa stuffing ((bits >> 12) | 0x3ff0..., minus 1 - 2^-53) and stored directly; normals use NumPy's ziggurat tables with a sign-folded table, a loop unrolled by four over a stack word buffer, and an out-of-line slow path whose fixed-point wedge brackets avoid most exp() calls. Platform tricks: madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) on outputs of 4 MiB or more on madvise-mode Linux kernels, and DC ZVA cache-line zeroing for large uniform fills on Apple Silicon.
when_to_use: R simulations that must give identical numbers regardless of thread count, worker scheduling or call order (future/parallel maps): hand each task a key from rng_key(seed, n) or rng_fold().

Bulk fills of 1e6+ uniforms or normals in R on a multi-core machine: it is the only R package in its benchmark that threads at the R level (1801 M/s uniform on 4 EPYC 7763 cores; 4984 M/s uniform and 3143 M/s normal on an 8-core M1).
Single-threaded R code that currently calls runif()/rnorm() in hot loops and can switch API: about 8x (uniform) and 13x (normal) faster than base R on the EPYC runner.
R packages with C code that need per-thread random fills or streamed chunks that never hold the full vector in memory (zurand.h fill_*_at, stream_normal).
Very long virtual vectors read only in part (lazy vectors: x[1:1e6] of a lazy 1e8 vector took a tenth of the time of generating the 1e8).
when_not_to_use: Code that must reproduce existing set.seed()/runif() streams, or users who expect the global-RNG API: values and interface both differ, and changing engine or normal method changes every value.
C or C++ projects outside R: there is no standalone library (zurand.h includes Rinternals.h and keys come from R); use Randompack's C library, simdrng or Random123 directly.
Distributions beyond uniform, normal, bounded integer and raw bits (no exponential, gamma, binomial, sampling); dqrng and randompack cover more.
Small single-threaded fills: against randompack the lead is 1.01-1.08x on normals and 0.97x for 1e5 uniforms on the M1, and fills under 32,768 values never thread.
Risk-averse production use: version 0.1.0 created in September 2026, not yet on CRAN, 0 stars, a single author; PractRand depth so far covers only the default engine (1 TB; 512 GB for normals).

integration.form: R package (compiled shared library loaded by R; C API header inst/include/zurand.h for LinkingTo packages)
integration.dependencies: R only at run time (no Imports); OpenMP optional (on macOS configure links the libomp that R ships); bundles Random123 (BSD-3), NumPy ziggurat tables (BSD-3) and fdlibm exp/log1p
integration.min_toolchain: Minimum R version not documented (DESCRIPTION has no Depends); a C compiler R can use; AVX2 path needs GCC or Clang (target attribute, __builtin_cpu_supports); macOS OpenMP needs the mac.r-project.org OpenMP headers at build time
integration.platforms: Linux (glibc and musl), macOS, Windows; x86_64 with optional AVX2 chosen at run time, aarch64 with NEON (DC ZVA on Apple only), scalar elsewhere; bit-identical output on all of these, 32-bit x87 excluded
integration.thread_safety: R samplers parallelise internally with OpenMP above 32,768 values (rng_threads() caps it, values unchanged); C API fills call no R API and may run from any thread once zurand_get_api() and key_get() have run on the main thread; each fill uses about 40 KB of stack (about 100 KB for positional fills and streams).

gotchas: Harness flaw in the x86_64 peer comparison: the workflow installs CRAN randompack 0.1.10, whose src/Makevars.in (since commit b8fe640, 2026-04-22) compiles no avx2.o and never defines BUILD_AVX2, so its x256++simd engine on x86_64 runs the fallback of eight interleaved scalar xoshiro256++ streams; the vignette's 'both vectorise the generator (AVX2 on x86_64)' is wrong for that build, and the 1.26x uniform and 1.03x normal leads on the EPYC 7763 are over randompack's non-SIMD path. The Apple M1 rows (NEON on both sides: 1.15x uniform, 1.01-1.03x normal, 0.97x at 1e5) are the like-for-like ones.

The published numbers use default arguments only: rng_uniform(key, n, min, max) with other bounds and rng_normal(key, n, mean, sd) with mean != 0 or sd != 1 add a second full pass over the output (two-wide, FMA-free by design), which no benchmark row measures.

On Linux kernels in transparent-huge-page madvise mode (the Ubuntu default) zurand itself requests 2 MiB pages for outputs of 4 MiB or more and the competitors do not; on a Neoverse N2 without the request it is at parity with randompack (268 vs 271 M/s uniform). options(zurand.hugepages = FALSE) turns it off; the EPYC runner used THP 'always', so its rows are page-size fair.

The default xoshiro256pp engine reaches a scattered position by reseeding and stepping up to 511 times; for random-index reads of lazy vectors key with engine = "philox4x64" (7-11x faster per read). Benchmarking a devtools::load_all() build measures an -O0 build about ten times slower.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick zurand over dqrng or randompack's R package when you need multi-threaded R-level fills or results that are bit-identical across thread counts and platforms with key-based substreams; pick Randompack (C library, R, Python, Julia, Fortran) for many distributions or non-R use, and OpenRAND or Random123 when you want counter-based generators in plain C++.
verified_claims_summary: R-level fills of 1e7 doubles, every package in one bench::mark() call, median of five rounds, R CMD INSTALL -O2 build with the compiler not named: on a GitHub-hosted AMD EPYC 7763 (AVX2, THP always) zurand xoshiro256pp gave 864 M/s uniform versus CRAN randompack x256++simd 688 (its scalar fallback on x86_64), dqrng 368 and runif() 104, and 366 M/s normal versus 355, dqrng 143, RcppZiggurat 125 and rnorm() 28; on a local Apple M1 2196 versus 1918 uniform and 739 versus 718 normal. Threaded rows (1801 M/s on 4 EPYC threads, 4984 on 8 M1 threads) compare zurand's OpenMP fills with single-threaded competitors.
status_note: Actively developed (183 commits between late September and 2026-10-05, many co-authored with an AI coding assistant per the commit log), MIT, version 0.1.0 installable from GitHub but not yet on CRAN; streams carry a version tag so later fixes will not change existing keys' values; its x86_64 lead over randompack is measured against randompack's non-SIMD CRAN build, so treat the M1 margins (1.01-1.15x) as the honest peer gap.
